                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6)
options(width = 100)

This vignette reproduces the classical analysis of the `sapi` series (six
trend and seasonal structures crossed with three calendar designs, 18 models
fitted to 2004--2024 and tested on 2025), adds lunarcast to it, and then shows
why a single test year is not enough to compare them.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(lunarcast)
adha  <- holiday_dates("idul_adha")
fitri <- holiday_dates("idul_fitri")
train <- window(sapi, end = c(2024, 12))
test  <- window(sapi, start = c(2025, 1))
```

## Six structures and three calendar designs

Each model is a regression with ARIMA errors on the original scale, so the
holiday effects are additive and the same in every year. The six structures
combine a trend and a seasonal component:

| Model | Trend | Seasonality |
|:--|:--|:--|
| m1 | deterministic ($\beta_0 + \beta_1 t$) | 11 monthly dummies |
| m2 | deterministic | Fourier terms, $K = 5$ |
| m3 | stochastic (differencing) | 11 monthly dummies |
| m4 | stochastic | Fourier terms, $K = 5$ |
| m5 | deterministic | seasonal ARIMA |
| m6 | stochastic | seasonal ARIMA |

The calendar part $C_t$ has three designs:

| Design | `design` | Calendar part $C_t$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| D1, month dummy | `"dummy"` | $\alpha V_t$, with $V_t = 1$ if month $t$ contains Eid al-Adha |
| D2, lead--lag dummies | `"leadlag"` | $\alpha_{-1} V_{t+1} + \alpha_0 V_t + \alpha_{+1} V_{t-1}$ |
| D3, proportional windows | `"window"` | $\alpha_{\text{before}}\,\mathrm{PRE}_t(w) + \alpha_{\text{holiday}}\,\mathrm{HOL}_t$ |

In D3, $\mathrm{PRE}_t(w)$ is the share of the $w$ days before Eid al-Adha
that falls in month $t$ and $\mathrm{HOL}_t$ the share of the holiday and
the three tasyrik days (Bell and Hillmer, 1983). The window length $w$ is
chosen from 7, 14, 21 and 28 days: every structure ranks the four by AICc,
and the length chosen by most structures is used for all six.

```{r classic}
classic <- calvar_classic_all(train, adha, design = c("dummy", "leadlag", "window"))
classic
```

The AICc of the window lengths:

```{r window-aicc}
aicc_w <- reshape(classic$window_aicc[, c("model", "w", "AICc")],
                  idvar = "model", timevar = "w", direction = "wide")
names(aicc_w) <- c("model", paste("w =", c(7, 14, 21, 28)))
aicc_w
```

Five of the six structures prefer $w = 14$ days. Within every structure the
proportional windows give the smallest AICc of the three designs (for m6,
1593.2 against 1647.5 with the month dummy). The effect of the two weeks
before the holiday is small (about 6 index points for a full window) but the
holiday window carries 21 to 26 points, and it is spread correctly over two
months when Eid al-Adha falls at the end of a month. The lead--lag dummies
show the same thing more crudely: the months before and after the holiday
month have small positive effects. With seasonal ARIMA errors (m5, m6) part of
the holiday effect is carried by the seasonal autoregression, so the
estimated effects are smaller than in m1 to m4.

## lunarcast on the same data

```{r lunarcast}
lc <- lunarcast(train, list(adha = adha, fitri = fitri))
lc
```

## One test year: 2025

```{r test}
fc_classic <- forecast(classic, h = length(test))
fc_lc      <- forecast(lc, h = length(test))
acc <- do.call(forecast_accuracy,
               c(list(actual = test), fc_classic, list(lunarcast = fc_lc)))
acc[, -1] <- round(acc[, -1], 2)
acc[order(acc$RMSE), ]
```

```{r test-plot}
plot(test, ylim = c(0, max(test, fc_lc$mean) * 1.15), lwd = 2, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Index", main = "2025: observed and forecasts")
lines(fc_classic$m6_dummy$mean, col = "darkorange", lwd = 1.5)
lines(fc_classic$m6_window$mean, col = "darkorange", lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
lines(fc_lc$mean, col = "royalblue", lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("observed", "classical m6, month dummy",
                     "classical m6, proportional windows", "lunarcast"),
       bty = "n", col = c("grey40", "darkorange", "darkorange", "royalblue"),
       lwd = c(2, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5), lty = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
```

A single test year is a fragile basis for comparison. In 2025 Eid al-Adha
fell in June for the third year in a row, the ideal situation for a seasonal
ARIMA model, which simply repeats last year's June, so the classical m6 model
with the month dummy also does well, even better than with proportional
windows. The difficult years are those in which the holiday moves to another
month, and they do not occur every year.

## Fourteen test years: rolling origin

`rolling_origin()` refits every model at the end of each year from 2011 to
2024 and forecasts the following year, so that 14 test years (2012 to 2025,
167 months) are used. With proportional windows, the length of the window
before the holiday is chosen again by AICc at every origin. Running it for all
models takes some time; the results for `sapi` are stored in the package:

```{r rolling-read}
r <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "rolling_sapi.csv", package = "lunarcast"))
r$model <- factor(r$model, levels = unique(r$model))
s <- rolling_summary(r)
s[order(s[, "all"]), ]
```

The lunarcast rows differ only in how the seasonal structure is chosen: by
AICc (`lunarcast_aicc`), fixed without seasonality (`lunarcast_none`) or by
cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule (`lunarcast`, the
default). `lunarcast_split` gives Eid al-Adha the two windows of the
classical window design, the 14 days before the holiday and the holiday with
the tasyrik days, each with its own effect. The code that produced the file
is shown at the end of this vignette.

```{r rolling-plot}
yearly <- tapply((r$pred - r$actual)^2, list(r$year, r$model),
                 function(v) sqrt(mean(v)))
years <- as.numeric(rownames(yearly))
show  <- c("classic_m6", "classic_m6_window", "lunarcast")
plot(years, yearly[, "classic_m6"], type = "b", pch = 19, col = "darkorange",
     ylim = c(0, max(yearly[, show]) * 1.1),
     xlab = "", ylab = "RMSE", main = "RMSE per test year")
lines(years, yearly[, "classic_m6_window"], type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2,
      col = "darkorange")
lines(years, yearly[, "lunarcast"], type = "b", pch = 19, col = "royalblue")
legend("topleft", c("classical m6, month dummy", "classical m6, proportional windows",
                    "lunarcast"), col = c("darkorange", "darkorange", "royalblue"),
       pch = c(19, 1, 19), lty = c(1, 2, 1), bty = "n")
```

What the table shows:

* Proportional windows improve every classical structure. The best classical
  model is now m6 with proportional windows, with an RMSE of 7.30 instead of
  7.95 for the month dummy. Lead--lag dummies hardly help (8.05 for m6).
* The gain stays small in the months that matter: in holiday months the RMSE
  of m6 falls only from 20.25 to 19.66, because the effect is still the same
  in every year. lunarcast lowers the overall RMSE to 4.94 and the RMSE in
  holiday months to 8.30.
* The two classical windows do not help inside lunarcast either:
  `lunarcast_split` has an RMSE of 7.76, against 4.94 for the single window
  that lunarcast chooses by AICc, $(-3, +7)$, which also covers the week after
  the holiday. The option is there to reproduce a chosen window design, not
  as a better default.
* Choosing the structure by AICc picks seasonal ARIMA errors at most origins
  and gives a clearly worse forecast than cross-validation: a good in-sample
  fit is not the same as a good forecast.

The notebook that introduced the three designs evaluated test years 2019 to
2025 by the mean of the yearly RMSEs. On that protocol the package gives the
same values for the month dummy and the lead--lag dummies of m6 (7.06 and
7.20); for the proportional windows it gives 6.24 rather than 6.16, because
here the window length is chosen again at every origin instead of once from
the data up to 2024:

```{r rolling-2019}
r19 <- r[r$year >= 2019, ]
r19$model <- droplevels(r19$model)
rolling_summary(r19)[c("classic_m6", "classic_m6_leadlag", "classic_m6_window",
                       "lunarcast"), c("all", "mean_year")]
```

## How the rolling-origin results were produced

```{r produce, eval = FALSE}
hol  <- list(adha = adha, fitri = fitri)
spec <- classic$spec[classic$spec$design == "dummy", ]
classic_design <- function(design, suffix) {
  m <- lapply(seq_len(6), function(i) {
    force(i)
    function(y, h) forecast(calvar_classic(y, adha, spec$trend[i], spec$season[i],
                                           design = design), h = h)$mean
  })
  setNames(m, paste0("classic_m", 1:6, suffix))
}
classic_models <- c(classic_design("dummy", ""),
                    classic_design("leadlag", "_leadlag"),
                    classic_design("window", "_window"))

# the lunarcast variants share the calendar selected at each origin
lunarcast_variant <- function(...) {
  function(y, h) {
    base <- lunarcast(y, hol, select = "aicc")
    fit  <- lunarcast(y, hol, window = base$window, effect = base$effect, ...)
    forecast(fit, h = h)$mean
  }
}
lunarcast_models <- list(
  lunarcast_aicc  = function(y, h) forecast(lunarcast(y, hol, select = "aicc"), h = h)$mean,
  lunarcast_none  = lunarcast_variant(season = "none", select = "aicc"),
  lunarcast       = lunarcast_variant(),
  lunarcast_split = function(y, h)
    forecast(lunarcast(y, hol, window = list(adha = list(before = c(-14, -1),
                                                        holiday = c(0, 3)))),
             h = h)$mean
)
r <- rolling_origin(sapi, adha, c(classic_models, lunarcast_models), first = 2012)
rolling_summary(r)
```

The same code is in `data-raw/rolling_sapi.R` in the package repository.

## Reference

Bell, W. R. and Hillmer, S. C. (1983). Modeling time series with calendar
variation. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 78(383),
526--534.
